For young Catholics, finding a moment of silence can feel almost impossible. Between school, sports, friendships, notifications, and the endless scroll of social media, there always seems to be something demanding their attention.

But Eucharistic adoration offers something increasingly rare: time to stop, put down the phone and simply be with Jesus.

A new movie is bringing the transformative power of Eucharistic adoration to the big screen. “Adore Him: He is Here” uses firsthand accounts of real encounters and transformation and depictions of salvation history to portray the powerful love of God that is found in the Blessed Sacrament.

The docudrama features several prominent Catholic figures including Archbishop Paul Coakley of the Archdiocese of Oklahoma City, Archbishop Jose Gomez of the Archdiocese of Los Angeles, Father Chris Alar of the Marian Fathers of the Immaculate Conception, Curtis Martin, the founder of FOCUS, evangelist Chris Stefanik, and many more. 

The film will be in theaters across the United States Oct. 4–8. 

Mark Hart is the chief innovation officer at Life Teen International, a Catholic youth ministry that provides resources for youth ministry experiences in middle school through high school. 

In the film, Hart discusses the rise being seen in young people attending adoration and why the youth is in need of Jesus in the Blessed Sacrament.

Every economics textbook tells the same origin story. Before money, people bartered. The baker wanted shoes, the shoemaker wanted fish, and nobody could find a match, so humanity invented money to fix the inconvenience. Adam Smith popularised the story in 1776 and it has been repeated in classrooms ever since. How we actually got from swapping fish for shoes to money is far less certain, and that question has divided economists for more than a century.

Carl Menger, founder of the Austrian school, offered the most convincing account in 1892. Money was never invented or decreed. People traded for goods that were easier to trade on, such as salt, cattle and metals, and over generations the most marketable good won. Nobody planned it. Gold and silver came out on top because they were scarce, durable, divisible and hard to fake. Money, in this view, is a market good that emerged from the bottom up, and it does not require a pure barter economy to have existed, only people looking for the easiest thing to swap.

Two rival schools disagree. Credit theorists, from Alfred Mitchell-Innes in 1913 to anthropologist David Graeber in 2011, argue that money began as debt. They point to Mesopotamian temple scribes recording obligations on clay tablets around 3000 BC, and to anthropologist Caroline Humphrey's 1985 finding that no economy built purely on barter has ever been described. State theorists, following Georg Friedrich Knapp in 1905, go further and argue money is whatever the state declares it to be and demands in tax. That idea is the intellectual root of Modern Monetary Theory.

The Austrian reply is hard to dodge. Those Mesopotamian debts were measured in barley and silver, which means a commodity was already doing the job of money before the scribe picked up his stylus. Credit between neighbours works in a village, but it does not scale to strangers, and that is exactly where a market good takes over. And the state theory explains how governments can impose a money, not why anyone valued it in the first place. History keeps showing that when a state's money fails, people return to whatever the market trusts.

What he is pointing at is an old esoteric move: reading the body as the temple the myths were written inside. 

The scene he treats as a map is the Egyptian weighing, usually told as a judgment after death. He turns it inward and says the same image is a living circuit. 

The seated figure becomes the circle of Willis, the arterial ring at the base of the brain that feeds the mind. The ascending path becomes the current between heart and head. The three tassels become nerve stems. The feather becomes action returning with the blood. In that reading, “death” is not the point. Misalignment is. 

Speech, intention, food, and thought sit on the scale the way the heart sat before Ma’at. What you utter and what you swallow either tune the instrument or detune it. The twenty-eight-day ring and the twenty-one-day renewal are the lunar and blood mysteries written onto bone: seven, three times, the spine as a procession of figures, white and red as the two bloods that cleanse and carry. 

Whether or not the glyphs were drawn as an anatomy chart, the teaching underneath is older than the chart. Life lengthens when rhythm is remembered.

That is also why a reading like this rearranges the Bible. Esoterica has long treated scripture as encoded physiology: the temple as the body, the river from the throne as the current through the heart, the lampstand as the lighted mind, the seven as the stations of the spine. 

If the cycle begins on the day you are born, then astrology here is not fortune-telling. It is a clock for the missing notes, the colors, stones, and minerals he says the sunlight has to pass through because three signs were not seated in you at birth. Bare feet on the ground, face toward the sun, stone on the skin: crude language for a precise idea, that the soul stays in the body by staying in correspondence with earth, light, and season. 

To be "demood" in his phrase, is to fall out of the signs of nature and then call the static a demon. The hidden thing is not a secret society. It is that renewal was never only moral. It was circulatory. Every twenty-one days the blood offers a small resurrection. Every twenty-eight, the wheel turns. 

The one who can hear their own frequency, and feed what the cycle is asking for, is already inside the scripture the page was trying to describe.

Friday, October 2, 2026

Borne on the Wings That Stirred the Nest

Scripture Reading: Deuteronomy 32:10-12  (“King James Version”)

10. He found him in a desert land, and in the waste howling wilderness; he led him about, he instructed him, he kept him as the apple of his eye.
11. As an eagle stirreth up her nest, fluttereth over her young, spreadeth abroad her wings, taketh them, beareth them on her wings:
12. So the Lord alone did lead him, and there was no strange god with him.

Key Verse: Deuteronomy 32:11  (“King James Version”)

11. As an eagle stirreth up her nest, fluttereth over her young, spreadeth abroad her wings, taketh them, beareth them on her wings:

Note to reader: All verses quoted are from "King James Version."

When Jehovah Disturbs the Soft Place So You Can Fly

First, Deuteronomy 32:11–12 sits inside Moses’ song of witness. Israel was found in a “waste howling wilderness,” kept as the apple of Jehovah’s eye, then trained. The eagle does four things: she “stirs” the nest (comfort becomes impossible), “flutters” over the young (presence and example), “spreads” her wings (invitation and covering), and “bears” them (rescue when they fall). The point is not cruelty. The point is unused power. Nestlings do not discover flight while the lining is still soft. The same Lord who disrupts also catches. “So the Lord ‘alone’ did lead him, and there was no strange god with him.” Exclusive leadership and exclusive support belong together.

Second, the meditation insists that difficulty is not the absence of Jehovah’s arm but often the place where the arm is most felt. A burden and an underneath support can arrive in the same hour. That is why the Christian may “count upon Him to deliver” precisely when the position looks unparalleled.

Third, two images interpret the first. Comfort can become a canopy that stunts growth: shade that feels like friendship may keep a plant from sun, rain, and full bloom. And soldiers are not finished on parade grounds. Forced marches, rivers, mountains, and knapsacks of sorrow educate warriors. Jehovah is after graces that only heat and height will draw out.

The pastoral conclusion is therefore not “enjoy pain,” but “do not misread the stirring.” What feels like abandonment may be the beginning of flight, bloom, and battle-worthiness—because the same Parent who pushes also bears.

The Nest Was Mercy—and Then Mercy Changed Shape

Jehovah’s first work with Israel was finding and keeping. He circled, instructed, and guarded. The nest is real. There are seasons when the Lord lines your life with rest, provision, quiet fellowship, and a sense that the rock will not move.

Then the same love “stirs.”

Stirring is not the same as forsaking. The eagle does not abandon the cliff. She makes the familiar place unlivable so that unused wings will have to answer the air. Many believers interpret the first sharp stone in the lining as evidence that Jehovah has withdrawn. Moses says the opposite: the Lord who stirs is the Lord who flutters, spreads, takes, and bears. Disruption and deliverance are two motions of one Parent.

Notice the order. He does not bear first and stir later. He stirs, then remains present, then carries. Faith is often asked to flap before it feels the pinions underneath.

Exodus had already said the same thing from the other side of the Red Sea: “Ye have seen what I did unto the Egyptians, and how I bare you on eagles’ wings, and brought you unto myself” (Exodus 19:4). The destination of the stirring is not mere survival. It is “unto Himself.”

Voices That Have Walked This Path

Charles Spurgeon preached that the eagle makes the young uneasy because love will not leave them in indolence. Trouble, he said, is often the nest being stirred so that the soul will look above this world of care. He also warned that the worst thing that can happen to a Christian is a path made too smooth; a cross can be one of the Lord’s great blessings, because affliction drives us to the promise and exposes the weak places we would never have faced on a feather-bed. Soldiers, he insisted, are educated in battle, not at the barrack gate.

Oswald Chambers pressed the same truth from another angle. Jehovah does not give us an “overcoming life” as a cushion against strain; He gives us life “as” we overcome. “The strain is the strength. Where there is no strain, there is no strength.” Chambers would not let us treat Christianity as deliverance “from” trouble only. It is deliverance “in” trouble. Noble things are difficult; the difficulty is meant to rouse us, not to make us faint. When Jehovah gets a soul alone through disappointment or thwarted plans, that is often when He begins to teach what ease never could.

William Branham, preaching often from this very text, loved to call God “Jehovah Eagle” and His people eaglets. He described the mother beating her wings until the loose feathers fly—the doubts, the world-soft lining, the little isms that will not survive altitude—and then spreading those same wings as the Word and the Spirit. His pastoral burden was simple: if you are an eagle, do not live like a barnyard bird. Use the wings. Jump. The One who stirred is the One who said He would bear.

These men do not agree in every doctrine. They agree here: the Jehovah who loves you will not leave you untrained, and the Jehovah who trains you will not drop you.

What the Stirring Is For

The nest is stirred so that “hidden capacity” comes to light. You do not know you can fly until the edge is under your feet.

The nest is stirred so that “exclusive trust” is formed. “The Lord ‘alone’ did lead him.” Strange gods—self-reliance, former comforts, human shade-trees—cannot go with you into the air.

The nest is stirred so that “weakness becomes the meeting place of power.” “My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness” (II Corinthians 12:9).

The nest is stirred so that you learn to “wait and mount,” not merely to brace and endure: “But they that wait upon the Lord shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint” (Isaiah 40:31).

Additional Scripture for Meditation

Read these slowly, aloud if you can, over several days. Let one phrase stay with you.

Psalm 55:22 — “Cast thy burden upon the Lord, and he shall sustain thee: he shall never suffer the righteous to be moved.”

Psalm 91:4 — “He shall cover thee with his feathers, and under his wings shalt thou trust: his truth shall be thy shield and buckler.”

Isaiah 41:10 — “Fear thou not; for I am with thee: be not dismayed; for I am thy God: I will strengthen thee; yea, I will help thee; yea, I will uphold thee with the right hand of my righteousness.”

James 1:2–4 — “My brethren, count it all joy when ye fall into divers temptations; Knowing this, that the trying of your faith worketh patience. But let patience have her perfect work, that ye may be perfect and entire, wanting nothing.”

Hebrews 12:11 — “Now no chastening for the present seemeth to be joyous, but grievous: nevertheless afterward it yieldeth the peaceable fruit of righteousness unto them which are exercised thereby.”

I Peter 5:6–7 — “Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time: Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you.”

Deuteronomy 33:27 — “The eternal God is thy refuge, and underneath are the everla”

Questions and Answers

Q1. If Jehovah loves me, why does He make the nest uncomfortable?

A. Because love wants more for you than permanent infancy. Comfort that never ends becomes a canopy that stunts. The stirring is aimed at flight, fruit, and fitness for the next obedience—not at your destruction.

Q2. How do I tell the difference between Jehovah’s stirring and mere chaos, or the enemy’s theft?

A. Look for the other three eagle-motions. Does the Word still flutter over you? Is there a spreading of covering even while the lining is gone? Is there, sooner or later, a bearing—strength not from yourself, a catch you did not engineer? Jehovah’s disruptions usually press you “toward” Himself and holiness. Theft leaves you only emptied. Ask also whether the trial is drawing out patience, humility, and prayer, or only bitterness and strange gods.

Q3. What if I have already fallen off the edge?

A.  The text does not say the young never drop. It says the parent “taketh them” and “beareth them.” Falling is not the last word where the Lord alone is leading. Cry out. Cast the care. The everlasting arms were already underneath the burden.

Q4. Does this mean I should seek hardship?

A. No. Do not stir your own nest in presumption. Do not despise the soft season when Jehovah gives it. Receive the nest with thanks, and receive the stirring with trust. The eagle decides the hour. Your work is obedience in whichever hour you are in.

Q5. What are “strange gods” in a stirred season?

A.  Anything you clutch as savior besides the Lord: a person who was your shade, a job that was your security, a reputation, a routine of ease, even a former spiritual feeling. The verse is jealous. He leads alone.

Q6. How long does the fluttering last before the bearing?

A.  Scripture does not clock it. Israel’s wilderness was long. Paul’s thorn remained. The promise is not instant altitude; it is that you are not unaccompanied in the air. Strength is given for the strain of the present minute.
How to Apply This in Daily Life

1. Name the lining that is being pulled out.

Write one sentence: “The nest-softness Jehovah seems to be removing is ______.” Do not spiritualize it into vagueness. Money, health, a relationship, a ministry door, a reputation, a habit of control—name it before Him.

2. Refuse the strange god of explanation-first.

You may never get a full “why” today. Practice “Thou alone” by praying Deuteronomy 32:12 when the mind races toward lesser trusts.

3. Use the small wings you have.

Do the next obedient thing while you still feel unready: the apology, the budget, the doctor’s visit, the unanswered prayer you keep bringing, the work of your hands. Flight is learned in short, awkward lifts, not in a single majestic circle.

4. Look for the flutter, not only the thrust.

Each day ask, “Where did the Lord stay present?” A verse that arrested you, a mercy you almost missed, a person sent, a restraint from sin. Stirring without noticing the flutter will make you bitter.

5. Cast the burden instead of decorating it.

Psalm 55:22 is not poetry for later. Speak the care out loud to Jehovah. Then act as one who has transferred the weight, even if feelings lag.

6. Let patience work.

James says the trying of faith works patience, and patience must “finish.” Do not demand instant bloom the week the oak is cut. Growth after shade is removed often looks worse before it looks glorious.

7. Become shelter for another eaglet.

Those who have been borne are to notice who is mid-air this week. A message, a meal, a silent sitting-with—this is how the church learns the Parent’s motion.

8. Keep the soldier and the plant in view without self-dramatizing.

You are not required to enjoy the forced march. You are required not to conclude that the march means you are unloved. Train in the actual duties of this day: truth-telling, purity, diligence, intercession. Warriors are made in ordinary faithfulness under fire, not in imagined heroics.

9. End the day under feathers.

Pray Psalm 91:4 at night. The same Jehovah who stirred the nest in the morning offers covering in the dark.

Lord, Thou foundest me in a waste place and keptest me as the apple of Thine eye. If Thou art stirring the nest, do not let me call Thy love by another name. Flutter over me. Spread Thy wings. When I drop, take me. Bear me. Lead me alone, and put away every strange god from my trust. Teach me to wait until I mount, to run without pretending I am not tired, and to walk when flying is not yet given. Underneath are the everlasting arms.

When Jehovah brings a child into unparalleled difficulty, that child may still count on being delivered—not always “out” of the air at once, but “in” the air, on wings that first disturbed the nest. The stirring is not the last thing He does. It is how He teaches you that you were never only a nestling. You were meant to ride the high places, and to know that the Lord alone did lead you.
In what area of your life right now are you experiencing the "stirring of the nest," and how can you lean into the training rather than fighting the discomfort?

Prayer🙏: The Eagle’s Wing: A Prayer on the Training of the Wilderness

My merciful, omnipotent, and sovereign Heavenly Father, You found us in a waste howling wilderness—a desolate, wind-swept place where we were utterly exposed.   I ask Jesus Christ to forgive us of our transgressions.  And yet, in Your infinite mercy, You did not leave us to perish in the dust. You kept us as the apple of Your eye, shielding us with Your grace, breathing life into our dry bones, and marking us as Your own.

You brought us out to bring us in, but You knew that comfort is a slow poison to the soul. You knew that if we remained in the shallow nest of our own ease, our wings would never learn the sky.

Thank You that You love us too much to let us stay comfortable.

Your discipline is never born of cruelty or caprice; it is the holy awakening of unused power. Like the great eagle over her brood, You began to stir the nest. You made our security uncomfortable, breaking up the cushions of our complacency until remaining where we were became impossible, driving us toward the edge of the precipice.

When fear paralyzed our limbs, You did not abandon us from afar. You fluttered over Your young, showing us Your presence, hovering with a fierce, protective nearness, and modeling the courage You demand of us.
And then, You spread Your wings. You gave the grand invitation, calling us off the safety of the ledge into the vast, terrifying unknown, offering Your broad feathers as both a bridge and a covering against the storm.

And Lord, when our strength failed—when the wind proved too strong, gravity too heavy, and our fledgling wings began to tire—You did not let us crash to the rocks. You swept underneath us, bearing us upon Your pinions, carrying our weight when we could no longer lift a feather.

Forgive us for fighting the stirring of the nest. Forgive us for mistaking Your rigorous training for abandonment, when all along You were unlocking the strength You placed inside us. Teach our souls to trust the wind of Your Spirit, knowing that every trial is simply an invitation to soar.  I love You so much, Abba Father, and I offer myself to You through Yeshua HaMashiach, my Lord, Master, and Savior. Amen.

9 PM Top-of-the-Hour News

Renee Good's family is suing the Trump administration. She was shot and killed by a federal immigration agent in Minneapolis in January. The administration claimed Good tried to hit the agent with her SUV. Good's family argues her civil rights were violated.
Becca Good was Renee Good's partner and was there when she was shot...: “What happened to our family should not happen to any family, regardless of who you are, who you voted for, or what you believe. ”
The family demanding a jury trial and damages.

Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has halted all executions, after convicted killer Christa Pike survive the state's lethal injection attempt.
Journalist Catherine Sweeney was a witness.: “I covered all the executions last year and most of the ones this year. We haven't seen anything like it. It went really poorly. ”
Pike was alive and snoring loudly after two doses of pentobarbital. Her lawyers, who have filed fore a stay of execution, say she likely suffered brain damage.

The Massachusetts judge who oversaw Lindsay Clancy's murder trial has rejected her lawyer's request to declare her not guilty of murder.
The judge ruled that prosecutors presented sufficient evidence for a jury to find her responsible for killing her three young children in 2023.
Her trial ended in a hung jury.

In Denton, Texas President Trump toured the Peterbilt Motors facility and told workers the stock market is through the roof and poverty numbers are low.: “There are more people working in the United States right now than at any time in the history of the United States. ”
Trump's stop in Texas is part of a broader tour touting the nation's economy ahead of the midterms. Tomorrow, the President will be in Mobile, Alabama to celebrate the groundbreaking of Mobile's new four-billion-dollar bridge.
There's no TV pool traveling with the President after CNN was removed from its scheduled rotation.

An Iowa teacher has been fired for offering students a quid pro quo.: “Substitute teacher Stephanie Mullally was planning a medical mission to Ecuador. She offered her students at Clinton Community School extra credit if they made donations on her personal GoFundMe page. The school district fired her for allegedly violating its ethics policy. A judge denied her attempt to collect unemployment benefits, ruling she had unfairly pressured her students to give money. Michael Wallace, Worldwide News Network. ”

A piece of history is now sealed beneath the Washington Monument for the next 250 years.: “With American and British military bands playing, officials lowered a joint time capsule beneath the Monument Plaza on Tuesday. Inside are letters from President Trump and Vice President JD Vance, a proclamation from King Charles, soil connected to George Washington, and essays from American students. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum says. The capsule represents two countries looking ahead together. This will carry forward the story through time of Americans and the Britons that will gather together to celebrate the nation's 500th birthday, and stamped on the capsule itself, do not open until July 4th, 2276. Stacy Lynn, Worldwide News Network, Washington. ”

text:
BRANIFF HISTORY TODAY - On this day, Wednesday, October 1, 1969, Braniff International inaugurated new nonstop service between Dallas Love Field and Miami International Airport; between Miami and New Orleans Moisant International Airport; and New Orleans and Dallas Love Field. The new service resulted from the Civil Aeronautics Board's findings in the Southern Tier Nonstop Investigation Case.

Local traffic service between New Orleans and Dallas had been inaugurated earlier on September 23, 1969, and an additional nonstop was added on October 1, bringing the total flights to five daily roundtrips between the two cities. One of the New Orleans flights also continued to Hawaii, via Dallas, and could now carry local passengers between Love Field and New Orleans. Braniff offered three daily roundtrips between Miami and Dallas Love Field including one nonstop and two single-stop flights. Two of the Miami to Dallas flights provided daily service to Hawaii. Between New Orleans and Miami International Airport, Braniff inaugurated two daily nonstop roundtrip flights.

Additional nonstop service from Tampa/St Petersburg/Clearwater, Florida, to Dallas Love Field, Miami International, and New Orleans Moisant was inaugurated at a later date. Braniff's new service was operated using Boeing 707 long-range four-engine jets and Boeing 727 Trijet aircraft.

On July 25, 1969, the Civil Aeronautics Board awarded Braniff International four new routes as a result of the Southern Tier Competitive Nonstop Investigation Case. One of the routes awarded was a crucial link between Dallas Love Field and Miami, that the carrier had long-sought since 1946, and had vitally needed since 1948, when the company inaugurated its first service to South America. The new route would directly link Dallas/Ft Worth, for the first time, with Braniff's Latin America route network that operated from the Northeast via the Miami Gateway.

However, for a brief period beginning on August 3, 1951, the CAB awarded Braniff single-plane service between Dallas and Miami, via Houston to help the airline feed its Latin America route system, and to stem the losses that were being experienced over these routes. However, Braniff was not awarded the authority to carry local traffic between the two points, which ultimately yielded the route unprofitable and it was canceled two years later on September 15, 1953. However, the nonstop service between Houston and Miami remained as well as nonstop service from Miami to Havana and Panama City/Balboa City, in the Canal Zone.

In the Board's final ruling, Braniff was awarded nonstop service from Dallas Love Field to Miami/Ft Lauderdale; Miami/Ft Lauderdale to New Orleans; New Orleans to Dallas; Tampa/St Petersburg/Clearwater and Miami, New Orleans and Dallas; and effective September 23, 1969, Braniff could begin carrying local traffic passengers between New Orleans and Dallas on its one-stop service from New Orleans to Hawaii. Beyond the local New Orleans-Dallas-Honolulu local traffic service that began on September 23, the remainder of the new service was inaugurated on October 1, 1969. The Board also required that all three of the new segments must ultimately serve the Dallas/Ft Worth area.

Braniff's new Southern Tier service was awarded just three days after the final award was granted for service to Hawaii, on July 22, 1969. Braniff President Harding L. Lawrence released a statement to the press that expressed his excitement about the new route award, "We are very pleased with this award, which will enable Braniff to provide nonstop service between any pair of these important cities and link them with the entire Braniff system. We look forward to implementing service under the new award, which is effective September 23." The new service would also create additional traffic at three (New Orleans, Miami, and Dallas) of the five coterminals (New Orleans, Miami, and Dallas, Atlanta, and Houston) that Braniff had been awarded in the Hawaii Service Case.

In a memo to employees, President Lawrence noted that the new Miami to Dallas link would create traffic beyond the two points. The route would connect the Southeast with Braniff services to Hawaii, Rocky Mountains, Pacific Northwest, Southwest, and Midwest creating a healthy flow of additional traffic to further boost Braniff's route system. Specific examples of Braniff destinations that enjoyed single-carrier and in many cases single-plane service to Miami, New Orleans, and Tampa, included Amarillo, Lubbock, Seattle, Denver, Portland, Tulsa, and Oklahoma City. Boeing 727 and 707 luxury jet aircraft were used on the new route awards.

Photo: Braniff International McDonnell-Douglas DC-8-62 Intercontinental Jet registered as N1804 is on pushback at Miami International Airport in 1970. The luxurious long-range airliner is painted in the famous 1967 Alexander Girard/Harper and George New Dark Blue Solid Color Scheme. The DC-8-62 was the backbone of Braniff's Latin America Division from 1967 until 1982.

text:
BRANIFF HISTORY TODAY - On this day, Saturday, October 1, 1966, Braniff International inaugurated jet service at Memphis and Nashville, Tennessee. Both Lower Mississippi Valley cities received Boeing 727-100 Trijet service which was welcomed with inaugural ceremonies to celebrate Braniff's historic new service.

At Memphis, Mayor William B. Ingram was presented with a beautiful plaque featuring a Braniff International Boeing 727-100 on the front, which was presented to him by Braniff Vice President Corporate and Marketing Planning John W. Leer. A special breakfast party was also held in honor of Braniff's new Memphis/Shelby County jet service.

The inaugural flight at Nashville Metropolitan Airport was welcomed with a spectacular civic luncheon for Braniff and city officials. On board the flight, ensuring that Braniff's inaugural was perfect on the in the air and on the ground, were Hostesses Sue Whitney, Bonnie Fuestel, and Cynthia Ray.

Braniff offered a daily eastbound morning Boeing 727 departure that originated at Dallas and then continued to Memphis and Nashville, where it arrived before noon and then continued to Washington National and Newark. An early afternoon departure originated at San Antonio every day and stopped at Dallas Love Field before continuing to Memphis and Nashville, arriving in time for dinner, before continuing to National and Newark. A late night departure originated at Houston, every day, and flew to Love Field before continuing to Memphis and Nashville, after midnight and then continued to Washington and Newark.

Westbound service also featured three daily flights that operated over the same routings. Departures were late night, early morning and afternoon, offering passengers the best times for business in either of the new jet service cities. Braniff's new service was a resounding success with with load factors well above Braniff's average.

Photo: Braniff International Boeing 727-27C Quick Change Convertible Cargo/Passenger Trijet registered as N7287 is taxiing at Memphis Shelby County Airport in August 1969. This jet is painted in the 1967 Alexander Girard/Harper and George Red Color Scheme.

Braniff International introduced the Boeing 727 into the fleet in May 1966, with the arrival of Ship N7282 which was a new Boeing 727-162 ordered by Pacific Northern but taken up by Braniff. In 1971, Braniff embarked on a Fleet Standardization Plan that aimed to reduce the number of aircraft types that the Dallas-based carrier operated to three. Boeing 727 for Mexico and Domestic US; Douglas DC-8 for South America, and Boeing 747 for Hawaii, were the types that best fit Braniff's needs during the 1970s and early 1980s.

You asked why people stay away, I think these are why. They can be overcome but for some reason people don't know it. HVAC/Electric/Plumbing has moats handyman doesn't. 

-That's fine. But generally good talent sought a license in a trade because they are self-motivated. Handyman talent pool is a little more opaque. I found success in identifying handymen with good reputations and seeking to acquire them. 

-Inefficiency: an electrical company or plumber has a finite set of things they do and the materials/fittings they carry are finite because of code. So they can carry more reliable inventory on their trucks. Handyman carry some, but what exact materials they need from day to day can be wildly variable. Being selective in what you offer and using tech to help with materials can reduce this quite a bit. 

-I started with $30k and ran one truck to $160k in first 12 months. The work and margins are there. I chose not to put capital in and am doing something else. 

I think its a good business

Real securities.
AMM liquidity.

Now look at what XRPL has been building.

Credentials.
Permissioned Domains.
Permissioned DEX infrastructure.
Multi-Purpose Tokens.
RLUSD.
Native exchange infrastructure.
XRP auto-bridging.

XRPL’s Permissioned Domains are specifically designed to let financial institutions restrict access according to credentials while still operating on the public XRP Ledger.

That is a very clean fit with the type of market structure the SEC is now allowing.

And XRP itself sits in a different regulatory bucket.

The SEC’s March 2026 interpretation was subsequently described in an SEC-filed Bitwise XRP ETF prospectus as expressly identifying XRP as an example of a digital commodity, with the filing stating that XRP itself does not constitute a security based on its current characteristics and publicly available information about XRPL.

So imagine the architecture:

Tokenized Apple shares = security
OUSG = tokenized Treasury exposure
RLUSD = digital dollars
XRPL = settlement and trading infrastructure
XRP = native liquidity asset

Those things do not need to compete with each other.
Each can do its own job.

And XRPL already has pieces of this happening.

Ondo’s OUSG Treasury product is on XRPL with RLUSD-based 24/7 minting and redemption.

Guggenheim Treasury Services brought Digital Commercial Paper to XRPL through Zeconomy.

The instrument had already processed more than $280M of issuance before expanding to XRPL.

So regulated U.S.-linked financial instruments are already touching the network.

Now take the SEC’s tokenized-stock model and scale it.

Stocks.
Bonds.
Funds.
Commercial paper.
Treasuries.
Stablecoins.
Tokenized deposits.

Every additional asset creates another market that needs buyers, sellers and liquidity.

XRPL’s auto-bridging can use XRP between two assets when the XRP route offers the better path:

Asset A → XRP → Asset B

That becomes interesting very quickly when hundreds or thousands of different tokenized assets exist.

You don’t need a perfectly liquid direct pair between every single asset.

Market makers can hold XRP inventory and use it as working liquidity.

And that kind of demand is completely different from someone buying XRP and waiting.

It becomes:
“We need XRP inventory to run the market.”

The SEC is also working on the issuance side through Regulation Crypto Assets, with proposed fundraising pathways of up to $5M over four years and up to $75M in a 12-month period under specified conditions. 

So America is addressing both ends:

how assets can be created onchain
and
how assets can trade onchain.

Ripple already has Payments, Custody, Prime, Treasury, RLUSD, tokenization infrastructure and XRPL positioned around that transition.

I’m bullish on $XRP because I’ve researched the infrastructure underneath this shift, not because Paul Atkins mentioned XRP. He didn’t.

I’m watching the rules being written for markets XRPL was already preparing to serve.

Study the filings yourself.
Study the tech.

Then decide how much of this thesis you agree with.

text:
The session was a bond-market story. The 10-year Treasury yield spiked to about 5.34%, the highest since 2002, then reversed and closed near 5.25%

The S&P bounced more than 60 points off morning lows once yields eased. 

Oil stayed the inflation input: WTI settled at $92.87, up $2.45 or 2.71%; Brent settled at $102.31, up $4.28 or 4.37%, back above $100 on China suspending oil-product exports and reports the US may send additional forces and a carrier toward the Middle East.

Data did not cool the inflation debate. September ISM manufacturing was 54.5 versus 55.0 expected, but prices paid jumped to 77.9 from 71.1. Jobless claims were 197,000 versus about 200,000 expected. August construction spending rose 0.9%. 

Tech, software, semis, industrials, and energy led the afternoon recovery. Banks, homebuilders, and REITs lagged the rate shock. Europe was hit harder (London about -1.7%, Paris about -1.6%).

What mattered for prices
•  Accenture $ACN jumped about 16% after a beat and fiscal 2027 revenue growth guidance of 3% to 6%, above the Street midpoint. Software was the cleanest pocket of strength.
•  Micron $MU beat and guided above views, with long-term supply agreements covering a large share of revenue, and finished up about 3% after an early fade. The AI memory bid held, but the bar is high after a huge year-to-date run.
•  Constellation Energy $CEG rose after a 20-year Amazon power purchase agreement covering 690 MW of nuclear capacity at Calvert Cliffs, including an uprate. Power-for-AI remains a live trade.
•  Mattel $MAT jumped on a takeover offer above $20 a share, implying a valuation around $6 billion.
•  Synopsys $SNPS rallied on investor-day targets (fiscal 2027 revenue around $11.1 billion to $11.2 billion, about 15% growth). Optical and memory names (including Coherent) also led.
•  $GOOG Gemini 4 Argon launch and continued AI infrastructure headlines (including Broadcom financing talk around Anthropic) kept the mega-cap AI complex in focus even as the index itself barely moved. Nike reported after the bell and was among the most active after-hours names

New highs and lows for October 1: 

NYSE 16 new 52-week highs and 394 new lows; 
Nasdaq 82 new highs and 528 new lows; NYSE American 1 new high and 29 new lows. 

Combined, new lows outnumbered new highs by roughly 9 to 1. That is not a healthy confirmation of the index bounce. 

The advance was narrow (software, semis, energy) while rate-sensitive and smaller names kept printing lows. Internals still argue the multi-week yield shock is doing more damage under the surface than the S&P close shows.

text:
1. The Fear of Being Led Astray (John 10:1-5).

Biblical Context: Jesus employs the Good Shepherd and the sheep metaphor to illustrate how His followers discern His voice and flee from strangers. The passage unveils a gripping psychological tension between trust and fear—between recognizing whom to follow and the apprehension of being misled.

Literary Parallel: Odysseus and the Sirens (Homer, The Odyssey). In The Odyssey, Odysseus faces the psychological trial of resisting the Sirens’ call. Like the sheep in John 10:5 who flee from a stranger’s voice, Odysseus must discern whom to listen to and avoid. He binds himself to the mast, symbolizing the human struggle against deception. The fear of being misled by false teachers (in John) or enchanting voices (in Homer) reflects the same psychological dilemma.

Philosophical Parallel: Plato’s Allegory of the Cave (The Republic). Plato describes prisoners who are accustomed to shadows and struggle to recognize the truth when confronted with reality. The prisoners’ lack of discernment resembles those in John 10, who must learn to recognize the true shepherd’s voice. The psychological fear of deception and the challenge of discernment are central themes in John and Plato’s work.

2. The Security of Belonging (John 10:7-9).

Biblical Context: This passage emphasizes the psychological comfort of having a safe passage and a protective leader. The need for security, belonging, and assurance is evident in this passage, reflecting the deep human desire to be part of something greater and the psychological implications of this desire.

Literary Parallel: Jane Eyre’s Search for a Home (Jane Eyre by Charlotte Brontë). Jane experiences profound psychological turmoil as she seeks a place where she is accepted and protected. Her longing for a home mirrors the sheep’s need for a shepherd. Just as Jesus offers security, Jane finds safety and belonging with Mr. Rochester.

Philosophical Parallel: Aristotle on Friendship (Nicomachean Ethics). Aristotle argues that friendship provides a sense of security and belonging, similar to how Jesus describes His relationship with His followers. The psychological assurance of a safe and meaningful relationship is central to John 10 and Aristotle’s ethical framework.

3. The Willingness to Sacrifice for Others (John 10:11-15).

Biblical Context: Jesus states, “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.” Selflessness highlights the psychology of self-sacrifice—choosing to endure suffering for the sake of others.

Literary Parallel: Sydney Carton in A Tale of Two Cities (Charles Dickens). Sydney Carton sacrifices his life for Charles Darnay, embodying the same willingness to die for another. His famous last words, “It is a far, far better thing that I do than I have ever done,” echo the Good Shepherd’s theme of sacrificial love.

Philosophical Parallel: Kierkegaard on Self-Sacrifice (Works of Love). Søren Kierkegaard emphasizes love as self-sacrifice, aligning with the Good Shepherd’s role in John 10. He argues that true love requires giving oneself completely, a theme that resonates deeply with Jesus’ declaration.

George Orwell once wrote, "If liberty means anything at all, it means the right to tell people what they do not want to hear." That principle cuts both ways, and it requires subjecting every narrative to basic scrutiny.

The fundamental problem with this post from @TuckerCarlson is not that rural farm violence is imaginary. Families living in remote parts of South Africa face terrifying break ins, genuine trauma, and reckless political rhetoric. That fear is completely real.

The real breakdown is the total lack of journalistic friction and cross examination.

Look at @piersmorgan. Morgan can be loud, chaotic, and obsessed with viral fireworks, but nobody gets an unchecked free pass on his show. He throws counter arguments into the room, demands receipts, and challenges basic facts in real time. Tucker offers a calm sit down, but nodding along to every single statement turns an interview into an echo chamber where unvetted assertions pass as objective gospel.

That complete lack of pushback is how you end up with wild factual errors slipping straight through to the audience, like Tucker asserting that Nelson Mandela was arrested for trying to bomb a train. It is basic history, yet nobody in the room stopped to correct it.

When you prioritize anecdote over actual data, the entire picture gets warped. The episode leaves out the demographic reality on the ground: the majority of victims who live, work, and die in these rural attacks include Black farmworkers and security staff, not solely white landowners.

The national numbers tell the true story. South Africa suffers through an overwhelming crisis of over 27,000 homicides every year. Murders on farms account for roughly 50 of those cases, about 0.2 percent of the national total. Independent criminologists confirm these are brutal, opportunistic armed robberies targeting isolated cash and weapons, not a state directed project.

If this were truly a systematic campaign of "white genocide" or "ethnic cleansing," global bodies like the United Nations, Amnesty International, and Human Rights Watch would be sounding the alarm. They track atrocities across the globe, yet none classify this crisis under those terms because the evidence of organized extermination is entirely absent.

Rural safety in South Africa is an urgent crisis, but treating "ethnic cleansing" and "white genocide" as undisputed facts collapses under empirical scrutiny. If a narrative is solid, it should easily survive a counter argument.

That's a great question. I am of the opinion that if it gets bad enough, it is at least grounds for separation, but not divorce unless she commits adultery. Other than that, a man ought to use all truth and pursuasion in wisdom and reason to convince her, and this is most effective when she can clearly see his gentle longsuffering spirit and dilligence in tending to her well-being. 

It is not for the faint of heart, and it is best for a man to choose a wife who is already convinced of the order of creation and her rightful role in the marriage. Unfortunately, what works in theory often fails to survive the confrontation with the real world, and whether it is passive aggression or outright rebellion, almost all women, even the best of intentioned women will resist the will of their husband. 

It is his responsibility to win her over and not to break her, to convinince her without coercion, and to find ways to make her *want* to submit. Done properly, it should be a shared joy and a burden less than the tension of a power struggle. More than anything, it takes time and navigating the rigors of life with wisdom and understanding. 

My wife and I were married a good six years before she genuinely began to submit out of a genuine spirit of trust and gratitude, and those first six years were rough, as they often are with any marriage. These days she is grateful for my leadership and trusts me enough to know that I am the one responsible not only for her physical and psychological well-being, but for her very soul, and I bear that burden gladly before Christ. 

We have been married 12 years now, and we almost never fight, though we do not always see eye to eye. But she submits out of love and faithfullness to me, knowing that not only is she responsible to submit, but that I am worthy of her submission.  

There is no "one size fits all", and it looks different in each context, but at the end of the day, it is the only paradigm that actually works and honors God, and by His grace and mercy, we are what we are in His sovereign hand. And in that comes the only liberty that is worth knowing, a life worth living together, and a companionship more fulfilling than anything the world has to offer.

text:
These states started in mid-to-late September, mostly as in-person absentee or early voting 45–46 days before Election Day:
•  Minnesota — in-person absentee voting began September 18. A separate early-voting period more like Election Day voting starts October 16.
•  South Dakota — in-person absentee began September 18.
•  Virginia — early in-person voting began September 18 in offices closed on the 19th; the official 45-day period started September 19 and runs through October 31.
•  Idaho — grouped with those states by the Center for Election Innovation & Research as starting September 18. Availability can vary by county.
•  Vermont — in-person options opened around September 19, when ballots became available (Vermont mails ballots to active voters).
•  Illinois — the state window opened September 24. Collar counties started then at clerk offices. Chicago opened in-person early voting on October 1 at the supersite (137 S. State St.) and the Board of Elections office (69 W. Washington St.). Suburban Cook County starts October 7; broader satellite sites in Illinois generally expand October 19.
Not yet open on October 1
The next statewide openings are later in the first half of October, including California (October 5), Indiana (around October 6), Arizona (October 7), and a large group around October 19 (Alaska, Arkansas, Connecticut, Colorado, and others). Alabama, Mississippi, and New Hampshire do not offer no-excuse early voting.

ZB30 REPORTING LIVE FROM RALEIGH: NORTH CAROLINA STILL LETS YOU SUE THE HOMEWRECKER

Good evening. I am standing outside the North Carolina State Capitol, where I can confirm that it is October 1, 2026, and in this state an affair is still something a jury can put a price on. Down to the dollar. Sometimes literally one dollar. More on that shortly.

THE TWO TORTS

North Carolina keeps two old common law claims that most of the country retired decades ago.

Alienation of affection: a spouse sues a third party for destroying the marriage. Under state case law, the plaintiff must show a marriage with genuine love and affection, that the love was alienated and destroyed, and that the defendant's wrongful and malicious conduct caused it. The defendant does not have to be a lover. It just usually is.

Criminal conversation: despite the name, it is a civil claim, not a criminal charge, and nobody has to converse. The plaintiff must show an actual marriage and sexual intercourse between the defendant and the plaintiff's spouse during the marriage. Two elements. That is the whole checklist.

THE EXCLUSIVE CLUB

North Carolina is one of six states that still allow alienation of affection suits. The others are Hawaii, Mississippi, New Mexico, South Dakota and Utah. Indiana became the first state to ban these claims in 1935. England, where the idea started with a 1745 case, abolished it in 1970. North Carolina looked at all of that and kept the receipts. An ABA Journal report from 2010 put the number of these suits filed in the state at more than 200 a year.

THE PRICE BOARD

No official menu exists. ZB30 built one from court records and press reports.

2011, Wake County: a judge awarded a jilted spouse $30.162 million against the woman who later married her ex husband. That was $10.162 million compensatory plus $20 million punitive. The defendant did not appear. Reports called it the largest award of its kind in state history.

2010, Guilford County: a jury awarded $9 million, $5 million compensatory and $4 million punitive, against a college administrator who skipped the trial and had no lawyer. Her quoted reaction: "I don't have a lot of money, so where this $9 million comes from is kind of hysterical." The verdict survived appeal in 2014.

2018, Durham County: a judge awarded a husband $8.8 million from his wife's boyfriend, $2.2 million compensatory and $6.6 million punitive, calling it "a textbook case" of how not to end a marriage in North Carolina.

October 2025, Carteret County: a jury awarded $5,562,000 against a neighbor in the same subdivision. Court summaries list the plaintiff's pretrial demand at $200,000 and the highest offer at $20,000. Phone records reportedly showed 40 hours of calls in the final two months. This reporter has confirmed that $200,000 is less than $5,562,000.

November 2025, Durham County: a jury ordered a TikTok creator with nearly 3 million followers to pay $1.75 million: $1.5 million for alienation of affection and $250,000 for criminal conversation.

September 24, 2026, Davidson County: a jury ordered a former NASCAR driver to pay $50,000 for alienation of affection, $800,000 for criminal conversation, and $1 in punitive damages on each claim. Total: $850,002. This reporter has checked the math. The two dollars are not a rounding error.

THE FINE PRINT, CIRCA 2009

On October 1, 2009, exactly 17 years ago today, the General Assembly added G.S. 52-13. Three rules. First, nothing a defendant does after the couple physically separates, with intent that the separation be permanent, can create a claim. Second, you have three years from the defendant's last act to file. Third, you can only sue a natural person. You may not sue the office holiday party. Only the coworker.

THE REPEAL WATCH

In 1984 the Court of Appeals tried to abolish these claims and the state Supreme Court reversed it, and in 2017 the Court of Appeals rejected a facial First Amendment challenge. Lawmakers keep trying. Senate Bill 626 was filed in March 2025 and sent to the Rules committee. Senate Bill 836, filed April 27, 2026, would repeal G.S. 52-13 and abolish both torts. Its last recorded action, on April 28, 2026, was a referral to Appropriations/Base Budget. As of tonight it has not passed the Senate. Both torts remain fully operational.

Residents are advised to treat flirting as an uninsured financial instrument.

text:
[There’s been too many cute and wholesome fics, so here’s some angst.]

A few days before the match against Ravenclaw, Harry finds himself walking down to dinner alone. Ron had made it only halfway down the spiral staircase from the boys’ dormitory before turning and bolting for the nearest lavatory. Hermione had departed almost as abruptly, clutching her Arithmancy essay and explaining that Professor Vector had to see a correction before she marked it.

She had asked whether he would go straight to the Great Hall. He had said he would, and at the time he had more or less meant it. Then the folded parchment in his pocket begins to occupy his thoughts before he reaches the first staircase.

It will only take a minute to check. That’s what he generally tells himself, although a minute has a way of becoming twenty when Malfoy is involved.

It has become a habit that Harry prefers to call it an investigation, though Hermione had pointedly referred to it as an obsession.

Whatever it is, Harry finds his hand slipping beneath his robes almost as soon as he turns down the next corridor. He withdraws the Marauder’s Map, unfolding it as he does. He taps it with his wand and speaks the familiar words under his breath.

His eyes are seeking one name in particular. Dracona Malfoy is not there. Crabbe and Goyle are easy enough to locate, lumbering together towards dinner, but Dracona’s name appears nowhere near them. There’s nothing particularly unusual about failing to find her and the map has been frustrating him for weeks. Nevertheless, the familiar irritation tightens under his ribs. Under that irritation, he can’t stop the small undercurrent of worry.

Harry tells himself, as he always does, that this is because Malfoy is up to something.

That is the only reason.

It has nothing whatsoever to do with how he immediately notices whenever she’s absent from meals, or how easily he can pick her white-blond head out of the Slytherin table from halfway across the Great Hall.

It certainly has nothing to do with the uncomfortable, inexplicable twist low in his stomach whenever he catches sight of her looking thinner than she had been at the beginning of the year, her once immaculate appearance increasingly frayed around the edges.

Those are details relevant to the investigation and nothing more.

Harry is just about to fold the map when his gaze finally catches upon a familiar name one floor below.

Dracona Malfoy

There she is. She is standing motionless inside a bathroom, and another name hovers near her, that of Moaning Myrtle. He descends the marble staircase two steps at a time, crosses the landing below, and makes his way along the passage toward the bathroom where he had seen Malfoy’s dot.

Only then does he properly notice the sign on the door, and his hand stops short of the handle. Following Malfoy into the girls' bathroom is the sort of thing Hermione would have a great deal to say about, and none of it would be favourable. On top of that, Harry can already imagine how it would sound if Malfoy told the story first.

For a moment he considers just waiting in the corridor, but first he leans forward, putting his ear almost against the door. Inside he can hear running water, faint but steady, followed by a sound that makes him stop thinking about explanations altogether.

At first he mistook it for Myrtle. The ghost’s usual complaints often rise and fall in much the same way. This sound is lower, caught painfully behind someone’s teeth, and interrupted by a breath drawn too quickly to fill the lungs. He presses his ear completely to the wood and hears Myrtle speaking in a voice softer than any he’s heard from her before.

“Don’t do that to yourself.” There’s a small, watery movement on the other side, and Myrtle continues, “Tell me what’s wrong. You can tell me, you know. I can help if you’ll only tell me.”

Harry eases the handle down. He slips just far enough inside to see the sinks, and stops with his fingers still curled around the handle. Malfoy stands with her back to him, leaning so heavily over one basin that her shoulders seem to be holding up the rest of her body.

Her robes hang crookedly from her shoulders. Beneath them her white shirt is creased and the green-and-silver knot of her tie is askew. Her hair, usually so carefully arranged, has come loose in tangled lengths.

Her hands grip opposite edges of the sink with such force that the knuckles look almost as white as the porcelain. Water runs beneath her bowed head, washing past a stain near the plughole, and every few seconds her arms tremble.

“I can’t do it,” she says. The words come out broken, barely louder than the tap, and she swallows before trying again. “I can’t. It won’t work. I’ve tried everything, and it still won’t-”

Her breath catches, cutting the sentence apart, and Harry feels his fingers tighten on the door. Malfoy is crying. He takes one silent step farther into the room and finally sees her reflection.

Tears stream down her pale cheeks and drip from her chin into the grimy basin. Black mascara has run beneath her eyes, streaking downward in thin, messy trails. Her silver eyes are swollen, and every few seconds she clenches her teeth as though desperately attempting to regain control.

Myrtle drifts out from one of the cubicles, her translucent spectacles catching a dull reflection from the lamps.

“Then don’t,” she offers, with the earnestness of someone who had discovered a perfectly simple solution. “Whatever it is, just don’t do it.”

Malfoy gives a laugh so short and broken that Harry wishes she hadn't tried.

“I don't want to do it.” She says it with a frightened emphasis, as if admitting that much is somehow worse than admitting failure. Her head bows lower, hiding her face from the mirror. “I don't want to, Myrtle. I don't want any of it.”

“Then tell someone,” Myrtle says, “There must be somebody.”

A single question bursts from Dracona with such bitterness that Myrtle recoils slightly.

“Who?”

Dracona lowers her head even further, and her hair spills forward over both shoulders.

“Who am I supposed to tell?” she whispers. “My mother? She already knows enough to be terrified every time an owl arrives. My father?”

Her fingers flex against the sink. “He’s in Azkaban because he failed. That’s the whole reason this is happening. I’m supposed to fix what he ruined.”

Harry’s heartbeat changes and he stands perfectly still.

Dracona continues before she can fully process what she had said.

“I thought I could do it,” she whispers. “I thought I had to. Everyone kept looking at me like I should be proud, like this was some great honor, and I pretended it was because what else was I supposed to do?”

Her voice cracks, and another sob escapes despite her effort to swallow it.

“I thought there would be another way,” Dracona whispers. “I kept thinking if I could just make it work, nobody else would have to be involved. But it won’t work, and if I fail-”

Her shoulders begin shaking again.

Myrtle moves closer. “What happens if you fail?”

Dracona stares down into the basin. Her reflection trembles across the thin layer of water beneath the tap.

“He kills me.”

Harry stops breathing.

“He kills my mother,” she continues. “And maybe Father, if he ever gets out. He said he would.”

Her mouth twists, fighting another sob. “He said this was my chance to prove that the Malfoy’s are still useful.”

Harry knows who she means. She doesn’t need to say a name. A strange sensation spreads through his chest, part horror, part vindication, part something he has no name for. He had been right. Malfoy is involved with Voldemort.

He should feel triumphant. Harry had spent months thinking of Malfoy as a willing conspirator, somebody delighted to prove herself worthy of joining the Death Eaters, and now he had proof. Yet the girl standing before him looks as though the weight of the task is crushing her piece by piece.

Myrtle says something Harry doesn’t catch. Dracona shakes her head, her hair brushing the wet basin, and the movement seems to exhaust her. When she speaks next, the effort has gone out of her voice, leaving it small and horribly matter-of-fact. “I'm on my own. Whatever happens, I'm on my own.”

Dracona draws a long, unsteady breath and lifts her head. Her gaze moves towards her own reflection, stops, and fixes on the dark-haired figure visible over her shoulder.

In the faded mirror above the sink, silver meets green.

Her eyes widen until the grey irises seem almost lost within them. The color drains from her already pale face, and her lips part soundlessly. Harry has never seen anyone look so utterly exposed. Black streaks from her ruined mascara mark both cheeks beneath those enormous, despairing eyes, her hair hung wild around her shoulders, and the haughty mask she had worn for as long as Harry has known her simply does not exist.

For one suspended moment, they simply stare at one another.

Harry does not see the girl who had mocked Ron’s family, laughed at Hermione’s blood status,  sneered at Hagrid or spent six years making herself one of the most infuriating people Harry had ever met.

He sees a terrified girl backed into a corner and believing she’s completely alone with no escape.

And Harry, without understanding why, has the overwhelming urge to tell her that she’s wrong.

Dracona’s expression empties with shock before something harsher rushes in to cover it, and he sees the moment she understands that he had heard her.

“Malfoy,” he begins, lifting his free hand a little. “I wasn't-”

She turns so sharply that her hair whips across her cheek, while her hand swiftly reaches into her robes. Harry knows that movement well enough for his own body to answer it before his mind catches up. His wand is in his fingers as she spins away from the mirror.

Her wand is in her hand, black against her fingers, and the look she gives him makes the rest of his explanation die in his throat. Anger tightens her mouth, but it arrives too late to hide everything else. Behind it is the same naked alarm he had seen in the mirror, now directed entirely at him.

“Get out!” Her voice cracks on the demand, and Harry sees her eyes flick to his raised wand.

He has time to say, “Wait, just stop-” before the black wand in her hand snaps towards him and a jet of light strikes the lamp beside the door, which shatters in a spray of glass and sparks.

Harry flings himself sideways as glass and metal scatter across the doorway, one hot fragment catching his sleeve before dropping away. He lands badly on his shoulder and rolls, bringing his wand up out of instinct.

Levicorpus, he thinks, aiming at the shape of her through the sudden dimness. He just needs her to stop, he just needs a moment to speak with her.

Dracona brings up a shield at the last possible instant, and the spell ricochets away into the ceiling, knocking loose a shower of dust and plaster.

Harry scrambles behind the nearest bathroom stall just as another curse strikes where his head had been a moment earlier.

The rubbish bin explodes.

Metal clangs across the tiles as scraps of paper, damp rubbish, and shattered pieces of the container scatter through the room. The blast leaves Harry’s ears ringing, and before he can recover, Myrtle’s shrill voice rises over everything.

“No! Stop it! Stop fighting!” She swoops between the stalls and sinks, hands pressed against the sides of her head. “Stop! STOP! You’ll destroy everything!”

Dracona barely seems to hear her. Her face has transformed completely.

The crying girl Harry had watched in the mirror has vanished beneath something wild and defensive. Harry knows Malfoy’s sneer. He knows the slow, superior smile she uses whenever she thinks she has found some new way to irritate him. He knows the gleam in her eyes when she is enjoying herself.

None of that is present now. She looks hunted.

“Expelliarmus!” Harry shouts.

Dracona twists aside and the spell clips the edge of a sink, blowing  a porcelain chunk from it.

“Impedimenta!”

Harry throws himself behind a cubicle partition just in time to dodge.

“Malfoy!” He shouts, wiping his lenses with his sleeve as he crouches behind the partition. “Just listen to me!”

“Why?” Dracona screams. “So you can run to Dumbledore? So you can tell Weasley and Granger?”

Harry tries to reason with her. “I haven’t told anyone!”

“You will!” She snaps back.

“You don’t know that!” He says.

“I know you!”

The answer strikes Harry with surprising force.

Dracona appears around the end of the cubicles.

Her wand is raised, but her hand trembles so badly that its tip shakes.

“You’ve spent six years hating me,” she says, her voice cracking. “You’ve spent this entire year following me. You wanted proof. Congratulations, Potter. You were right.”

Harry pushes himself upright. “I didn’t know-”

“You never know anything,” Dracona says through gritted teeth.

Harry lowers his wand slightly motioning at the surroundings. “You think I wanted to find you like this?”

Something changes in her face. “Don’t.”

Harry stops. “Don’t what?”

“Don’t look at me like that.”

He stares at her, slight confusion leaking into his expression. “Like what?”

Her face contorts with rage as she yells, “Like you pity me!”

Harry opens his mouth to protest, but she cuts him off immediately.

“Liar! Stupefy!” She screams with a force that scrapes her voice raw.

Harry jerks his wand across his body, deflecting the spell with a motion that sends a painful jolt through his wrist. The red flash hurtles towards the stalls, passes through Myrtle’s drifting shoulder, and shatters a cistern behind her. Porcelain flies in every direction, and water bursts out in a rush that strikes the floor and spreads beneath the stalls. Harry staggers as water surged around his shoes, carrying shards of debris along with it.

“STOP!” Myrtle screams. “STOP IT! STOP IT!”

Dracona fires another spell, but Harry smoothly blocks it. Blue light flashes against red, rebounding into one of the mirrors and cracking it from corner to corner.

Within seconds the bathroom becomes bedlam.

“Expelliarmus!”

Dracona blocks.

“Impedimenta!”

Harry twists away.

“Petrificus Totalus!”

“Protego!”

Magic bursts across the bathroom in violent flashes, reflected a dozen times in the surviving mirrors. Harry ducks beneath a curse that carves a smoking mark through a cubicle door, then sends another disarming charm toward Dracona that she knocks aside with a frantic sweep of her wand.

Their duel has none of the rhythm of practice. There are no measured attacks, no calculated counters.

Water streams from the ruined cistern and broken plumbing. Broken glass glitters beneath the shallow flood. Myrtle flies overhead in frantic circles, wailing at both of them while Harry and Dracona exchange spells through the chaos.

As Harry dodges around another spell, his heel lands on slick tile and his foot goes out from beneath him. Pain jolts through his back as he strikes the floor, and his wand nearly slips from his hand.

He looks up and finds Dracona standing a few paces away, her wand raised, the broken cistern still pouring behind her. Her robes have been soaked, and a wet strand of hair lays across her mouth, but she seems unaware of either.

There is none of her familiar satisfaction in having gained the advantage. Harry had seen Malfoy look pleased at his expense often enough to know the expression by heart, and this is something else entirely. Her silver eyes are wide, her breathing ragged, and terror has pulled every feature taut beneath the anger.

“Cruci-” she begins. The syllables scrape out of her, driven by panic and the need to make him stop looking, stop asking, stop standing so close to everything she can’t bear to have discovered. Her grip tightens, and she sees him flinch beneath the wand she has pointed at him. For that fraction of a second, she can no longer pretend he’s merely Potter, merely the enemy whose name gave her permission to do what she’s about to do.

What am I doing?

The thought strikes with such sudden clarity that her breath stalls. Harry is on the floor, one hand braced in the water, looking up at her through glasses that have slipped crookedly across his face. A face she knows far better than she had ever allowed herself to explain. The final syllables catch in her throat, and her wand hand falters.

Harry does not see the hesitation. He hears the beginning of the curse, and his body answers before fear can become anything as deliberate as a choice. There is no plan or conscious decision. Only the memory of cramped handwriting in the margin of an old Potions book.

For enemies.

“SECTUMSEMPRA!” he bellows. His arm sweeps upwards in a wild, desperate movement, the tip of his wand cutting across the space between them.

Dracona’s body jerks as though something has struck her across the chest, and a scream tears out of her with a violence that makes Harry’s own breath stop. Sudden red lines begin to appear from under her white shirt. She jerks backwards, and blood strikes the sink behind her in a scattered spray. A cut appears beneath one silver eye, sharp enough that Harry sees it form before he understands what he was seeing. Her free hand flies towards her chest and the wand in her right hand dips towards the floor.

Blood strikes the pale tiles beneath her, her knees give way, and she collapses into the water with an impossibly loud splash. The black wand falls from her hand and rolls away beneath a wash of pink, while her hair spreads around her head in pale, tangled lengths. For an instant her fingers still move, closing weakly against the floor, and then the water around her begins turning red.

Harry can only stare. His own arm is still raised, his wand pointing at the place where she had stood, and some part of his mind remains stupidly fixed on the expectation that she will get up. Her mouth opens instead around a desperate breath, and blood runs from the wound beneath her eye into the hair beside her face.

“No,” Harry says. It comes out as little more than air, and he pushes himself to his feet so quickly that he slips again, catching the edge of a basin before he falls. “No, Malfoy- I didn’t-”

He lurches towards her, splashing through water and broken porcelain, and drops to his knees hard enough that the impact ought to have hurt. He feels nothing beyond the sickening shock of reaching her and finding the blood warm against his hands. It has soaked the front of her shirt, stained the loosened green-and-silver tie, and spread beneath the edge of her robe. He presses his palm against the worst of it, then shifts it because another place is bleeding, then realises there is no position in which his hands can cover everything.

“I didn’t know,” he says. The words are too small, absurdly useless beside the wounds opening beneath them, but they are the only ones he can make himself say. “I didn’t know. I didn’t know that it would…”

Dracona shudders under his hands. The movement brings a thin, broken sound from her throat, and Harry snatches his palms back for half a second, terrified that he had hurt her more, before the fresh rush of blood makes him press down again.

Myrtle is screaming overhead. “Murder! Murder! There’s been a murder!”

“She’s not dead!” Harry shouts. The desperation in his own voice frightens him.

Harry bends closer to Dracona’s face, trying to see whether her eyes are still following him. They’re open, silver beneath lashes clumped with tears, but their focus slips past his shoulder before finding him again.

“I'm sorry,” he says, his voice thick with desperation. He sweeps wet hair from her cheek with the back of his wrist, leaving a red smear across her skin. “I'm sorry, I know. Just- just hold on. Please.”

Dracona trembles again. Harry slides an arm beneath her shoulders, meaning to lift her out of the cold water, and draw her awkwardly against him while trying to keep his other hand pressed to her chest. She is lighter than he expected. He had scarcely touched her except through the collisions and hostility that passed for contact between them, and some stupid part of him had assumed she would feel as immovable as she always tried to appear.

Her eyes move towards his face. Harry bends over her at once, holding his breath so that he could hear whatever she is trying to say. He sees her lips part with a faint, painful effort. He expects an accusation, his surname spoken with the last of her anger, or perhaps a plea for him to stop pressing against a place that hurt.

“I’m sorry,” she whispers. The words are quiet, yet he hears them with perfect clarity. Her gaze lingers on his for one brief moment after she says them, before slipping out of focus again.

Harry shakes his head. It‘s a small movement at first, before panic makes it sharper. Why is she apologising to him? He is the one with her blood on his hands.

“No, don’t say that. You haven’t- you don’t have to say that.” His fingers shift uselessly against the soaked cloth, and he looks from her mouth to her eyes, trying to find proof that she had heard him. “Dracona, please. Just stay awake.”

Her eyes open a fraction wider. She manages one coherent thought before consciousness leaves her.

He said my name.

The door slams open hard enough to strike the wall. Harry looks up so sharply that the movement tugs at his arm, and he immediately looks down again to make sure he didn’t hurt her.

Severus Snape stands in the doorway, his face rigid with fury, his black eyes taking in the shattered fixtures, red water, and the girl held against Harry’s blood-soaked chest. His wand is already drawn by the time he reaches them.

“Put her down.” Snape says in a low voice.

Harry blinks. “Professor, I-”

Snape drops to one knee beside him and repeats, with a force that finally breaks through, “On the floor, Potter. Now.”

Harry lowers Dracona onto the wet floor as carefully as he can, supporting her head until the back of it rests against her soaked robe. When he pulls his hands away, they leave bloody prints against her blouse.

His bloody hands remain lifted before him. He numbly stares at them.

Red has worked into every line of his palms, beneath his fingernails, across his cuffs. His robes are soaked in water and blood until the fabrics are almost indistinguishable.

Dracona’s blood.

Snape pushes Harry aside with one arm. His expression becomes intensely controlled, which somehow frightens Harry more than open anger would have.

He begins murmuring an incantation. His wand follows the course of each wound with exact care. Harry watches the tip move, willing it to work with such force that his own chest hurts. At first there seems to be no change at all.

On the second repetition, the edges of the wounds begin drawing together. Harry simply watches, a helpless frustration gnawing at him.

Snape performs the countercurse a third time. His voice never wavers, and when he finally draws his wand away he remains bent over her for a moment, examining what is left.

“Is she-” Harry begins. His gaze moves helplessly from her face to Snape’s. “Professor, is she going to be all right?”

Snape slides one arm beneath Dracona’s knees and the other behind her back.

“I was too slow to prevent scarring,” he says, in a voice so tightly controlled that Harry feels each word as an accusation. Snape lifts her from the floor, gathering her carefully against him, and the trailing edge of her robe sends a few red drops back into the water. “I am taking her to the hospital wing.”

Harry feels cold. His eyes immediately fix on the thin mark crossing Dracona’s cheek. She will have a scar.

The idea strikes with almost nauseating force.

Harry knows what it meant to carry evidence of someone else’s violence across your face. He knows what it means to wake up every morning and see it in a mirror.

Now Dracona would have one because of him.

Snape stops in the doorway. He looks back, and the cold fury in his expression holds Harry where he stands more effectively than a hand against his chest.

“And you, Potter,” he says, each word deliberate, “will wait here for me.”

It does not occur to Harry to disobey. He remains beside the broken cubicle as Snape carries her out, listening to the footsteps until he can't separate them from the running water.

Across the floor, crimson stains open and drift like flowers, their edges loosening as the water carries them around fragments of porcelain and the fallen black wand. Her apology won’t leave him.

Harry stares at his hands, still shaking too badly to hold them still.

What have I done?

The question circles without finding anywhere to settle, while Harry watches the crimson flowers spreading over the tiles. He can’t make sense of her saying she was sorry, or of the terror that had seized him when her eyes began to close.

But most of all, he can not understand why hurting Dracona Malfoy felt so much like reaching into his own chest and tearing out his heart.
